context: Single-view stipple dot map of U.S. population density; one dot = 10,000 people, rejection-sampled inside state boundaries; hover highlights a state's dots in blue while dimming others; ~33,000 total canvas dots rendered at 0.9px radius on a warm off-white background.
first_impression: The map reads immediately — dense dot clusters in the Northeast corridor, California coast, and Texas metros pop out against sparse interiors with no effort.
what_works: Monochromatic encoding eliminates color overload entirely, and the dot density directly encodes population spatially so the viewer needs no legend to extract the core insight. The canvas highlight interaction (selected state in blue, rest dimmed to 25% opacity) provides clean focus-plus-context without animation complexity.
what_doesnt: Northeast states are tiny hit targets — Rhode Island, Connecticut, Delaware, and DC are nearly impossible to hover precisely, undermining the per-state tooltip. The legend gives a dot-to-people ratio but no density scale or reference marks, so judging magnitude differences between, say, Ohio and Michigan requires the tooltip.
